title: Federal Procurement & Acquisition Essentials
blurb: Three days on the acquisition lifecycle, FAR-grounded practice, source selection, and contract management — taught by practitioners who have built national procurement systems from the ground up.

modules.t: Day 1A — The Federal Acquisition System & Integrity
modules.d: How the FAR system is built, who holds authority, the thresholds that change the rules, and the integrity framework behind every award.
modules.body:
Why federal acquisition is different

Federal acquisition spends public money under rules designed to deliver best value while ensuring competition, transparency, fairness and integrity. Private purchasing can simply choose a preferred supplier; a federal buyer must be able to show that the process was lawful, competitive where required, and documented so that auditors, oversight bodies and disappointed offerors can see how and why the decision was made.

The regulatory architecture

The Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR), codified in Title 48 of the Code of Federal Regulations, is the primary rulebook for executive-agency acquisitions. Agencies issue supplements — the Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS), and others for agencies such as GSA, HHS and DOE — plus internal policies. Statutes underpin the system, including the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA), the Procurement Integrity Act, the Contract Disputes Act and the Small Business Act. The FAR's traditional structure moves through the lifecycle: general matters and integrity (Parts 1–5), competition and planning (Parts 6–12), acquisition methods and contract types (Parts 13–18), socio-economic programmes (Part 19 onward), and contract management (Parts 42–51), with clauses in Part 52.

Regulatory status note (2025–26). The FAR is being rewritten under the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul (RFO). Since 2025, virtually all agencies have adopted model class deviations that reorganise and simplify FAR text; formal rulemaking began in June 2026 with proposed rules covering many parts, and final rules are expected to follow. This course uses the traditional FAR part numbers, which remain the common reference, and teaches durable principles. Before acting on any specific requirement, check the current FAR, your agency's RFO deviation text and its supplement (e.g., DFARS) at acquisition.gov.

Who can bind the government

Only a contracting officer (CO) acting within the limits of a written warrant can enter into, modify or terminate contracts on behalf of the government. Programme managers, contracting officer's representatives (CORs) and technical staff cannot — however senior. When someone without authority directs a contractor to perform work, the result is an unauthorized commitment, which can only be ratified by an official with authority under defined conditions (FAR 1.602-3). Unauthorized commitments are a recurring audit finding and can leave individuals personally exposed.

Thresholds that change the process

Dollar thresholds determine which procedures apply. Following the statutory inflation adjustment effective 1 October 2025, key thresholds include: the micro-purchase threshold, raised from $10,000 to $15,000 (purchases often made by government purchase card with minimal competition); the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT), raised from $250,000 to $350,000 (streamlined procedures under Part 13); the threshold for requiring certified cost or pricing data, raised from $2 million to $2.5 million; and the ceiling for simplified procedures for commercial products and services, raised to $9 million. Thresholds are adjusted for inflation every five years and some vary for specific purposes, so always confirm current values.

Competition: the default

CICA requires full and open competition unless a statutory exception applies (FAR Part 6), such as only one responsible source, unusual and compelling urgency, international agreement, or authorisation by statute. Using an exception requires a written justification and approval (J&A) at the appropriate approval level. Competition is not a formality: it drives price, quality and innovation, and protects the integrity of public spending.

Integrity framework

The Procurement Integrity Act (FAR 3.104) prohibits knowingly disclosing or obtaining contractor bid or proposal information or source selection information before award, and governs employment discussions between officials and offerors. FAR Part 3 also addresses gratuities, kickbacks, contingent fees and personal conflicts of interest; Part 9.5 addresses organisational conflicts of interest, where a contractor's other activities could impair objectivity or give an unfair competitive advantage. Ethics rules on gifts apply to every employee involved in acquisition.

Practitioner's lens. Systems built from the ground up — in the U.S. or in national procurement reforms abroad — succeed when integrity is designed into the process: segregated roles, documented decisions, controlled information and independent review. Procedures without integrity produce paperwork; integrity without procedures produces inconsistency. Federal acquisition needs both.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my federal acquisition coach. Give me eight short scenarios involving authority (who can bind the government), thresholds, competition exceptions and procurement integrity. For each, ask what the correct action or rule is. Then explain the answer with the relevant FAR part, remind me to confirm current thresholds and any RFO deviation text, and score my performance.

📚 Glossary

  • FAR: Federal Acquisition Regulation, 48 CFR
  • Contracting officer: official with warranted authority to bind the government
  • Unauthorized commitment: agreement made by someone without authority
  • J&A: justification and approval for other than full and open competition
  • Procurement Integrity Act: prohibits improper disclosure of proposal and source selection information
  • RFO: Revolutionary FAR Overhaul (2025–26)

📖 References

  • Federal Acquisition Regulation, 48 CFR Chapter 1 — acquisition.gov.
  • FAR Council — Revolutionary FAR Overhaul model deviation text and proposed rules (2025–26), acquisition.gov.
  • Inflation adjustment of acquisition-related thresholds, effective 1 October 2025 (41 U.S.C. 1908).
  • Competition in Contracting Act of 1984; Procurement Integrity Act (41 U.S.C. 2101–2107).

quiz.q: A programme director emails a contractor asking it to start an additional training module immediately, promising that 'contracting will sort out the paperwork'. What has MOST likely occurred?
opts: An unauthorized commitment, because only a warranted contracting officer can bind the government
A permissible exercise of an option
quiz.x: Only contracting officers within warrant authority can bind the government. Such commitments may require ratification under FAR 1.602-3.

quiz.q: Following the 1 October 2025 inflation adjustment, which statement about the simplified acquisition threshold is correct?
opts: It was replaced by the micro-purchase threshold
quiz.x: The SAT rose from $250,000 to $350,000; the micro-purchase threshold rose from $10,000 to $15,000.

quiz.q: An agency wants to award a contract without full and open competition because only one firm holds the required proprietary data rights. What is required?
opts: A written justification and approval citing the applicable statutory exception, approved at the required level
quiz.x: CICA exceptions in FAR Part 6 require documented J&As at appropriate approval levels.

quiz.q: During evaluation, an evaluator's friend at a competing firm asks how its proposal compares with others. What does the Procurement Integrity Act require?
opts: Share information after the competitive range is set
Do not disclose source selection information before award, and report the contact as required
quiz.x: Knowingly disclosing source selection information before award is prohibited; contacts should be reported.

quiz.q: A contractor that wrote the specifications for a system now wants to compete for its production. Which issue MUST be assessed?
opts: Organisational conflict of interest under FAR Part 9.5
quiz.x: Writing specifications can create an unfair competitive advantage or impaired objectivity — an OCI that must be addressed.

quiz.q: Which document is the PRIMARY rulebook for executive-agency acquisitions, alongside agency supplements?
quiz.x: The FAR is the primary regulation; supplements such as DFARS add agency-specific rules.

quiz.q: A contracting specialist finds that a FAR section quoted in last year's training manual has been reorganised under the RFO. What is the BEST practice?
opts: Check the current FAR, the agency's RFO class deviation text and its supplement before acting
Ignore the deviation until final rules are issued
Ask the contractor which version to apply
quiz.x: Agencies have adopted RFO class deviations; current text and supplements govern.

quiz.q: Which contract action could an agency typically make using a government purchase card with minimal competition procedures?
opts: A $12,000 commercial purchase within the micro-purchase threshold
quiz.x: Since October 2025 the general micro-purchase threshold is $15,000; larger actions require other procedures.

quiz.q: Why does federal acquisition require extensive documentation compared with private purchasing?
opts: Because the FAR forbids electronic records
Because public funds require demonstrable fairness, competition, legality and accountability to auditors and offerors
quiz.x: Documentation shows how and why decisions were made, supporting accountability and defence against protests.

quiz.q: A COR verbally tells a contractor to add features not in the statement of work. Who has authority to change the contract?
quiz.x: CORs have delegated technical monitoring authority but cannot change contract terms.

modules.t: Day 1B — Requirements, Market Research & Acquisition Planning
modules.d: Defining needs well, researching the market, applying small-business rules and building an acquisition strategy.
modules.body:
Most acquisition problems start with the requirement

Unclear, overly restrictive or shifting requirements cause delays, protests, cost growth and poor performance. Experienced contracting professionals invest heavily in requirement definition with the programme office, because everything downstream — competition, evaluation, contract type and administration — depends on it.

Describing the need (FAR Part 11)

Requirements should state the government's needs in terms of functions to be performed, performance required, or essential physical characteristics, and only include restrictive provisions to the extent necessary. Three common documents: a statement of work (SOW) specifying tasks, often detailed; a performance work statement (PWS) stating required outcomes and measurable performance standards, used in performance-based acquisition (FAR 37.6) and generally preferred for services; and a statement of objectives (SOO) stating high-level objectives and inviting offerors to propose their own PWS, which encourages innovation. Brand-name or overly specific requirements restrict competition and must be justified.

Market research (FAR Part 10)

Market research is required before developing new requirements and before soliciting offers above certain levels. It identifies available commercial products and services, typical industry practices, pricing, capable sources — including small businesses — and potential risks. Techniques include requests for information (RFIs), sources sought notices, industry days, reviewing existing contracts and GSA schedules, and consulting subject-matter experts. Results must be documented and should directly inform the acquisition strategy.

Commercial first. FAR Part 12 establishes a preference for acquiring commercial products and commercial services where they meet the need, using streamlined procedures and commercial terms. Market research determines whether commercial solutions exist; unnecessary government-unique requirements increase cost and risk.

Small business and the rule of two

Federal policy requires maximum practicable opportunity for small businesses. Under the rule of two, an acquisition above the micro-purchase threshold must generally be set aside for small businesses when there is a reasonable expectation that offers will be received from at least two responsible small businesses and award will be made at fair market prices (FAR 19.502-2). Programmes for 8(a), HUBZone, service-disabled veteran-owned and women-owned small businesses have additional authorities. Market research findings support set-aside decisions, and agencies work with their small business specialists.

The independent government cost estimate

An independent government cost estimate (IGCE) estimates what the requirement should cost, prepared independently of offerors' pricing. It supports budgeting, price reasonableness determinations and evaluation of proposals. Good IGCEs document assumptions, sources (historical contracts, market data, labour rates) and methodology.

Acquisition planning (FAR Part 7)

Acquisition planning integrates the efforts of everyone responsible for an acquisition to meet the need in the most effective, economical and timely manner. Written plans typically address background and objectives, the requirement, cost, capability and performance, delivery, trade-offs, risks, competition and sources, contract type, source selection approach, budgeting and funding, management of the contract, and milestones. Planning should start early — complex acquisitions can take a year or more.

Choosing the vehicle

Options include a new standalone contract, orders under existing indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity (IDIQ) contracts, GSA Multiple Award Schedule orders (FAR 8.4), governmentwide acquisition contracts (GWACs), blanket purchase agreements, or required sources (FAR Part 8). Using existing vehicles can save months but must fit scope, ordering procedures and fair-opportunity requirements.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my acquisition planning partner. I will describe a requirement. Help me decide between SOW, PWS and SOO; draft measurable performance standards; design a market research plan (RFI questions, sources sought, industry day); assess the rule of two; outline an IGCE with assumptions; and draft an acquisition plan outline under FAR Part 7, flagging what I must confirm in current FAR and agency supplements.

📚 Glossary

  • PWS: performance work statement with outcomes and measurable standards
  • SOO: statement of objectives inviting offerors to propose solutions
  • Rule of two: set-aside requirement when two or more responsible small businesses are expected
  • IGCE: independent government cost estimate
  • IDIQ: indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract
  • Market research: collecting and analysing information about capabilities in the market

📖 References

  • FAR Parts 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 19, 37 — acquisition.gov.
  • Small Business Administration — contracting programmes and set-aside guidance.
  • GSA — Multiple Award Schedule ordering guidance.
  • OFPP — Seven Steps to Performance-Based Acquisition.

quiz.q: A programme office requests a specific brand of laptop because 'staff like it'. Market research shows several products meet the functional need. What should the contracting officer do?
opts: Set aside the purchase for large businesses
Ask the brand's reseller to confirm
Describe the need in functional or performance terms unless a brand-name justification is legitimately supported
quiz.x: Requirements should not restrict competition beyond the government's actual needs; brand-name requires justification.

quiz.q: An agency wants vendors to propose innovative approaches to reduce help-desk wait times. Which requirement document BEST supports this?
opts: A detailed SOW prescribing every task
quiz.x: A SOO states objectives and invites offerors to propose their own solutions and PWS.

quiz.q: Market research identifies four responsible small businesses likely to offer fair market prices for a $1.2 million service. What does the rule of two generally require?
opts: A GSA order to a large business
A sole-source award to the cheapest firm
Full and open competition including large firms
quiz.x: A reasonable expectation of two or more responsible small business offers at fair market prices generally requires a set-aside.

quiz.q: Which statement BEST describes a PWS?
opts: A list of every task and method the contractor must use
A document prepared by the contractor after award
A statement of required outcomes with measurable performance standards
quiz.x: A PWS focuses on outcomes and measurable standards, supporting performance-based acquisition.

quiz.q: Why must the IGCE be prepared independently of offerors' prices?
opts: It must be kept secret from the programme office
Because offerors are not allowed to price
To provide an objective benchmark for budgeting and evaluating price reasonableness
quiz.x: An independent estimate allows objective comparison and price analysis.

quiz.q: An agency plans a complex IT modernisation and starts acquisition planning two months before funds expire. What is the MOST likely risk?
opts: Rushed requirements, weak market research and protest or performance risk
quiz.x: Complex acquisitions require early planning; rushing undermines quality and defensibility.

quiz.q: Market research shows a commercial service meets the need with minor tailoring. What does FAR policy favour?
opts: Acquiring the commercial service using commercial procedures where appropriate
Delaying until a custom design is approved
quiz.x: FAR Part 12 prefers commercial products and services where they meet the need.

quiz.q: Which market research technique is MOST useful for gauging whether capable small businesses exist?
opts: A sources sought notice requesting capability statements and size status
Requesting certified cost or pricing data
quiz.x: Sources sought notices identify capable sources and support set-aside decisions.

quiz.q: An agency wants to order cybersecurity services quickly through an existing IDIQ. What must be confirmed?
opts: That the order is under the micro-purchase threshold
That the work is within the IDIQ's scope and ordering procedures, including fair-opportunity requirements, are followed
quiz.x: Existing vehicles save time only if scope and ordering rules are respected.

quiz.q: Which element is NOT normally addressed in a written acquisition plan?
opts: Contract type and source selection approach
quiz.x: Plans address strategy before competition; naming a winner in advance undermines competition.

modules.d: Choosing the right acquisition method, structuring the solicitation, and allocating risk through contract type.
modules.body:
Matching method to the requirement

The FAR provides several acquisition methods. Micro-purchases (now up to $15,000 in general) use streamlined procedures, often the government purchase card, while spreading purchases among qualified suppliers. Simplified acquisition procedures (FAR Part 13, generally up to the $350,000 SAT, and up to $9 million for qualifying commercial acquisitions under the test programme) allow quotations and simpler evaluation. Sealed bidding (Part 14) suits clear, complete specifications where award is made on price and price-related factors to the lowest responsive, responsible bidder, without discussions. Contracting by negotiation (Part 15) suits complex requirements where technical approach, past performance and other factors matter, allowing discussions and best-value trade-offs. Orders under existing vehicles (Part 8.4, IDIQs, GWACs) are often fastest.

The structure of a solicitation

Requests for proposals under Part 15 commonly follow the uniform contract format: Part I (the schedule, sections A–H, including supplies or services and prices, description or statement of work, packaging, inspection and acceptance, delivery, contract administration data and special requirements), Part II (contract clauses, section I), Part III (attachments, section J), and Part IV (representations and instructions — section K representations, section L instructions to offerors and section M evaluation factors). Sections L and M must align: offerors should be asked to submit exactly what will be evaluated. Commercial solicitations use the simplified format under FAR 12.303 and the SF 1449.

Clarity reduces protests. Ambiguous evaluation criteria, inconsistent instructions, or requirements that conflict between the PWS and section M are among the most common sources of confusion and protests. A pre-release review by legal counsel and an independent contracting colleague is one of the highest-value hours in any acquisition.

Contract types: allocating risk

Contract type (FAR Part 16) allocates cost and performance risk between government and contractor. The objective is to negotiate a type and price that give the contractor the greatest incentive for efficient and economical performance, consistent with the risk.

  • Firm-fixed-price (FFP): the contractor bears full cost risk; preferred when requirements are clear and costs can be reasonably estimated. Commercial acquisitions generally use FFP or fixed-price with economic price adjustment.
  • Fixed-price incentive and fixed-price with economic price adjustment: share risk through targets or adjust for market factors such as commodity prices.
  • Cost-reimbursement types — cost-plus-fixed-fee, cost-plus-incentive-fee, cost-plus-award-fee: the government pays allowable costs plus fee; used when uncertainties prevent reliable cost estimates. They require that the contractor's accounting system is adequate for determining costs and that appropriate government surveillance is in place, and they impose more administrative burden.
  • Time-and-materials (T&M) and labour-hour: used only when it is not possible to estimate extent or duration accurately; least preferred, requiring a determination and findings that no other type is suitable, and a ceiling price the contractor exceeds at its own risk.
  • Indefinite-delivery contracts (IDIQ, requirements, definite-quantity): used when exact quantities or timing are unknown.

The cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost system is prohibited, because it rewards contractors for increasing costs.

Choosing well

Consider requirement maturity, price competition, cost estimation reliability, technical and schedule risk, the contractor's accounting system, the government's administrative capacity, and past experience. Starting a programme with cost-reimbursement during uncertain development, then moving to fixed-price for production as risks fall, is a common pattern.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my solicitation and contract-type advisor. I will describe a requirement, its value, maturity and risks. Recommend the acquisition method and contract type with reasoning, outline sections L and M so they align, identify any FAR prerequisites (e.g., determinations and findings, accounting system adequacy, ceiling prices), and list the five most likely sources of ambiguity a pre-release review should catch.

📚 Glossary

  • Sealed bidding: award to lowest responsive, responsible bidder without discussions
  • Uniform contract format: standard sections A–M for Part 15 solicitations
  • Section L / M: instructions to offerors / evaluation factors
  • FFP: firm-fixed-price contract
  • Cost-reimbursement: payment of allowable costs plus fee
  • T&M: time-and-materials, least preferred contract type

📖 References

  • FAR Parts 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 — acquisition.gov.
  • FAR 12.303 and Standard Form 1449 — commercial solicitations.
  • DAU — Contract types and source selection resources.

quiz.q: A requirement has clear, complete specifications, several qualified suppliers and no need for discussions. Award will be made solely on price. Which method is MOST appropriate?
opts: Contracting by negotiation with best-value trade-off
quiz.x: Sealed bidding suits complete specifications and price-based award without discussions.

quiz.q: An agency awards a contract where the contractor's fee is 10% of whatever costs it incurs. What is wrong?
opts: It is a prohibited cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost arrangement
Nothing, it is a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract
It is acceptable for commercial items
quiz.x: CPPC is prohibited because it rewards higher costs.

quiz.q: Development of a novel sensor has high technical uncertainty, making cost estimates unreliable. Which contract type is MOST suitable initially?
opts: A cost-reimbursement type, provided accounting system and surveillance requirements are met
quiz.x: Cost-reimbursement suits high uncertainty, with prerequisites for accounting systems and surveillance.

quiz.q: Section L asks offerors for a detailed staffing plan, but section M does not evaluate staffing. What is the MAIN problem?
opts: Instructions and evaluation factors are misaligned, creating confusion and protest risk
quiz.x: Sections L and M should align: request what will be evaluated.

quiz.q: Which contract type places the GREATEST cost risk on the contractor?
quiz.x: Under FFP the contractor bears the full risk of cost overruns.

quiz.q: A T&M contract is proposed for help-desk support. What does the FAR require?
opts: Certified cost or pricing data for every hour
A determination and findings that no other type is suitable, and a ceiling price
quiz.x: T&M is least preferred and requires a D&F and ceiling price.

quiz.q: A five-year contract for fuel delivery faces volatile commodity prices. Which type BEST addresses price volatility while retaining fixed-price discipline?
quiz.x: FP-EPA adjusts for specified market contingencies such as commodity prices.

quiz.q: A $280,000 commercial service purchase with straightforward requirements is planned. Which procedures are LIKELY available?
opts: Simplified acquisition procedures under FAR Part 13
Only Part 15 negotiation with full UCF
quiz.x: The purchase is below the $350,000 SAT, so simplified procedures are generally available.

quiz.q: Which section of the uniform contract format contains the evaluation factors?
quiz.x: Section M states the evaluation factors for award.

quiz.q: A programme starts with cost-reimbursement development and moves to firm-fixed-price production after design stabilises. Why is this pattern common?
opts: Because FFP is prohibited in development
Because contract type should match the level of cost and technical uncertainty, which falls as the programme matures
quiz.x: Risk allocation shifts as requirements mature and costs become predictable.

modules.d: Trade-off and LPTA, ratings and documentation, discussions, price and cost analysis, debriefings and protests.
modules.body:
Best value has two main routes

Under FAR Part 15, the government seeks the best value. Two approaches dominate. In the trade-off process, the government may award to other than the lowest-priced offeror or the highest technically rated offeror if the perceived benefits of a higher-priced proposal merit the additional cost — but the trade-off must be documented with a rationale. In the lowest price technically acceptable (LPTA) process, proposals are evaluated as acceptable or unacceptable against non-price factors, and award goes to the lowest-priced acceptable offeror; no trade-offs are permitted. LPTA suits well-defined requirements where higher performance has little value; statutory and policy restrictions limit its use for complex services, especially in defence.

Evaluation factors and the solicitation promise

Evaluation must follow the factors and their relative importance stated in the solicitation — section M is a promise to offerors. Price must always be evaluated; past performance is generally required for negotiated competitive acquisitions above the SAT unless documented as inappropriate; quality factors such as technical approach and management capability follow the requirement. Evaluators must apply ratings consistently, document strengths, weaknesses, significant weaknesses and deficiencies, and avoid using unstated criteria.

The documentation test. Could an independent reviewer — a GAO attorney or a judge — read the evaluation record and understand exactly why each proposal received its rating and why the award decision was made? Adjectival ratings alone ("Good", "Acceptable") are not enough; the narrative must explain the underlying findings and the trade-off reasoning. Most sustained protests involve inadequately documented or inconsistent evaluations.

Clarifications, competitive range and discussions

Clarifications (FAR 15.306(a)) are limited exchanges when award without discussions is contemplated — for example, resolving minor clerical errors or clarifying past performance information — and may not be used to cure deficiencies or materially revise a proposal. If discussions are needed, the CO establishes a competitive range of the most highly rated proposals, then holds discussions with each offeror in it, which must be meaningful: addressing deficiencies, significant weaknesses and adverse past performance information the offeror has not had a chance to address. Discussions are followed by final proposal revisions.

Price and cost analysis

The CO must determine that the price is fair and reasonable. Price analysis evaluates the price without evaluating its separate cost elements — comparing competing offers, prior prices, published price lists, the IGCE or parametric estimates; adequate price competition is usually the strongest basis. Cost analysis reviews individual cost elements and profit, required when certified cost or pricing data are obtained (generally above the $2.5 million threshold where no exception applies, such as adequate competition or commercial items). Cost realism analysis is required for cost-reimbursement contracts to determine the probable cost of performance and may be used in fixed-price competitions to assess understanding or risk.

Responsibility

Award may go only to a responsible prospective contractor (FAR Part 9): adequate financial resources, ability to meet delivery, satisfactory performance and integrity record, necessary organisation and controls, and eligibility. CO checks include the System for Award Management (SAM) exclusions and performance information systems. For small businesses, a non-responsibility determination is referred to the SBA for a Certificate of Competency decision.

Debriefings and protests

Unsuccessful offerors in Part 15 competitions may request a debriefing; a post-award debriefing request must generally be received within three days of notification of award. Debriefings explain significant weaknesses and deficiencies, the overall ratings and price of the awardee and the debriefed offeror, and the rationale for award — without revealing other offerors' confidential information. Good debriefings reduce protests. Bid protests may be filed with the agency, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) or the U.S. Court of Federal Claims. At GAO, protests of solicitation improprieties must generally be filed before the closing date; other protests generally within ten days of when the basis is known, with special timing rules after required debriefings. Timely GAO protests can trigger an automatic stay of award or performance under CICA.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my source selection reviewer. I will paste anonymised evaluation narratives and a draft award decision. Check whether ratings are supported by documented strengths and weaknesses, whether unstated criteria were used, whether the trade-off rationale is adequate, whether exchanges were clarifications or discussions, and whether price analysis supports fair and reasonable pricing. List the protest vulnerabilities and how to fix each.

📚 Glossary

  • Trade-off: award to other than lowest price or highest rated with documented rationale
  • LPTA: lowest price technically acceptable
  • Deficiency: material failure to meet a requirement
  • Competitive range: most highly rated proposals selected for discussions
  • Price analysis / cost analysis: evaluating total price / evaluating cost elements
  • Responsibility: capability and integrity to perform, assessed before award

📖 References

  • FAR Parts 9, 15 (15.101, 15.306, 15.404, 15.505–15.506) — acquisition.gov.
  • GAO Bid Protest Regulations, 4 CFR Part 21; GAO Bid Protest Annual Reports.
  • U.S. Court of Federal Claims — bid protest jurisdiction (28 U.S.C. 1491(b)).
  • DoD Source Selection Procedures (current edition).

quiz.q: Under a trade-off source selection, the government awards to a proposal priced 8% higher than the lowest-priced offer. What makes this defensible?
opts: The higher-priced offeror is an incumbent
A documented rationale showing the specific benefits justify the price premium
The lower-priced offeror is a small business
quiz.x: Trade-offs require documented reasoning linking benefits to the price difference.

quiz.q: In an LPTA competition, a proposal is technically superior and 3% higher in price than the lowest acceptable proposal. Who receives award?
quiz.x: LPTA permits no trade-offs; the lowest-priced acceptable proposal wins.

quiz.q: An evaluator downgrades a proposal for lacking an ISO certification that the solicitation never mentioned. What is the issue?
opts: Use of an unstated evaluation criterion
quiz.x: Evaluations must follow stated factors; unstated criteria create protest grounds.

quiz.q: The CO contemplates award without discussions but asks an offeror to fix a deficient technical approach. Why is this improper?
opts: Deficiencies can only be fixed after award
The CO should cancel the solicitation
Clarifications cannot be used to cure deficiencies or materially revise proposals; that would constitute discussions
quiz.x: Curing deficiencies is discussions; if held with one offeror, they must be held with all in the competitive range.

quiz.q: After establishing the competitive range, the agency holds discussions but does not raise a significant weakness in one offeror's proposal. What principle is at risk?
opts: Discussions must be meaningful, addressing deficiencies and significant weaknesses
quiz.x: Meaningful discussions must lead offerors into areas needing revision.

quiz.q: Five offerors compete for a firm-fixed-price contract with prices close together. Which is typically the strongest basis for a fair and reasonable price determination?
opts: Adequate price competition, documented through price analysis
quiz.x: Adequate price competition is usually the strongest basis and an exception to certified data requirements.

quiz.q: Which analysis is REQUIRED for cost-reimbursement contracts to determine probable cost?
quiz.x: Cost realism determines the probable cost of performance for cost-reimbursement contracts.

quiz.q: The apparent awardee, a small business, appears to lack financial capacity. What must the CO do if determining it non-responsible?
opts: Award to the next offeror immediately
Refer the matter to the SBA for a Certificate of Competency determination
quiz.x: Non-responsibility determinations for small businesses are referred to SBA.

quiz.q: An unsuccessful offeror wants a post-award debriefing. Generally, by when must the request be received?
opts: At any time before contract completion
Within 3 days of notification of award
quiz.x: FAR 15.506 generally requires the request within three days after notification.

quiz.q: An offeror believes the solicitation's evaluation criteria are unfair. When should a GAO protest of the solicitation terms generally be filed?
opts: Before the closing date for receipt of proposals
quiz.x: Protests of apparent solicitation improprieties must generally be filed before the closing date.

modules.d: Surveillance, changes, performance evaluation, payment, disputes, terminations and closeout.
modules.body:
Award is the beginning, not the end

Value is delivered — or lost — during performance. Contract administration ensures the government receives what it paid for, on time and within cost, while treating the contractor fairly under the contract terms. Poor administration produces cost growth, disputes and audit findings even after excellent source selections.

Roles in administration

The contracting officer retains authority over the contract. A contracting officer's representative (COR), designated in writing, performs technical monitoring: observing performance, inspecting deliverables, reviewing invoices for technical acceptance and documenting issues. The COR's designation letter defines limits — CORs cannot change price, quantity, delivery, scope or other terms. Programme staff should channel any desired change through the CO. A kickoff (post-award) conference aligns expectations on roles, communication, deliverables and invoicing.

Surveillance and quality assurance

For performance-based contracts, a quality assurance surveillance plan (QASP) describes how the government will monitor performance against the PWS standards — methods (100% inspection, random sampling, periodic inspection, customer feedback), frequency, acceptable quality levels and documentation. Inspection and acceptance follow the contract clauses (FAR Part 46). Acceptance generally becomes conclusive except for latent defects, fraud, gross mistakes amounting to fraud, or as otherwise provided by warranties.

Document as you go. Contemporaneous records — surveillance reports, correspondence, meeting minutes, deliverable reviews — are the government's evidence in disputes and performance evaluations. Problems discovered but not documented are almost impossible to act on later.

Modifications

Contract modifications (FAR Part 43) are written changes. Bilateral modifications (supplemental agreements) are signed by both parties — for example negotiated equitable adjustments or agreed changes. Unilateral modifications are signed by the CO alone — administrative changes, change orders under the Changes clause, and exercise of options. The Changes clause lets the CO order changes within the general scope of the contract; the contractor must proceed and is entitled to an equitable adjustment in price or schedule if the change affects cost or time. Changes outside the general scope — a cardinal change — are new work requiring competition or a justification.

A constructive change occurs when the government, without a formal change order, requires work beyond the contract — through informal direction, defective specifications, or overly strict interpretation. Constructive changes often arise from CORs or programme staff directing work, and can generate claims.

Options

Options may be exercised only in accordance with their terms, within the time specified, when funds are available, the need continues and exercise is the most advantageous method of fulfilling the requirement, considering price and other factors (FAR 17.207).

Performance evaluation and payment

Agencies record past performance in the Contractor Performance Assessment Reporting System (CPARS), evaluating quality, schedule, cost control, management, small business subcontracting and regulatory compliance. Evaluations must be accurate, evidence-based and timely; contractors may comment. Under the Prompt Payment Act, agencies generally must pay proper invoices within specified periods (commonly 30 days) or pay interest penalties.

Disputes, terminations and closeout

The Contract Disputes Act governs claims: contractor claims are submitted to the CO, and claims over $100,000 require certification; the CO issues a final decision, which may be appealed to a board of contract appeals or the Court of Federal Claims. Contracts may be terminated for convenience (government's right, with settlement of costs and reasonable profit on work performed) or for default (contractor failure, typically preceded by a cure notice for many failures). Closeout (FAR 4.804) confirms delivery, final payment, release of claims, de-obligation of excess funds and file completion.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my contract administration advisor. I will describe a performance situation (anonymised). Determine whether it involves a change within scope, a cardinal change, a constructive change or an unauthorized commitment; identify the correct modification type; outline the equitable adjustment considerations; state what must be documented; and draft a short, professional letter from the contracting officer to the contractor.

📚 Glossary

  • COR: contracting officer's representative for technical monitoring
  • QASP: quality assurance surveillance plan
  • Bilateral / unilateral modification: signed by both parties / by CO alone
  • Equitable adjustment: fair adjustment of price or schedule for a change
  • Constructive change: informal government action requiring extra work
  • CPARS: Contractor Performance Assessment Reporting System

📖 References

  • FAR Parts 4 (4.804), 17 (17.207), 33, 42, 43, 46, 49, and clause 52.243 (Changes) — acquisition.gov.
  • Contract Disputes Act (41 U.S.C. 7101–7109).
  • Prompt Payment Act (31 U.S.C. 3901–3907).
  • CPARS — guidance for assessing officials.

quiz.q: A COR tells a contractor to add weekend coverage not required by the PWS, and the contractor complies. What is the MOST likely legal characterisation?
opts: A constructive change that may lead to a claim
quiz.x: Informal direction requiring extra work can be a constructive change; CORs lack authority to change the contract.

quiz.q: The CO orders a change to delivery locations within the contract's general scope. The contractor objects to the extra cost. What should happen?
opts: The contractor may stop work until paid
The contractor proceeds and is entitled to an equitable adjustment if cost or time is affected
quiz.x: Under the Changes clause, the contractor must proceed; equitable adjustment compensates affected cost or schedule.

quiz.q: An agency wants to add a large new software development effort to a facilities maintenance contract. What is the PRIMARY concern?
opts: The change is a cardinal change outside the general scope, requiring competition or justification
quiz.x: Work outside general scope is new procurement, not a modification.

quiz.q: Which modification can the CO sign unilaterally?
opts: A settlement of a contractor claim
Exercise of an option in accordance with its terms
A no-cost scope reduction requested by the contractor
quiz.x: Option exercise and change orders are unilateral; negotiated agreements are bilateral.

quiz.q: A contractor submits a $250,000 claim to the CO. What does the Contract Disputes Act require?
opts: Certification of the claim, since it exceeds $100,000
Submission to the Court of Federal Claims first
quiz.x: CDA claims over $100,000 require certification.

quiz.q: Before exercising a contract option, which consideration is required?
opts: Funds are available, the need continues and exercise is the most advantageous method considering price and other factors
quiz.x: FAR 17.207 sets conditions for option exercise.

quiz.q: Monthly surveillance reports show recurring late deliverables, but the COR never documented them. At year-end the CO wants to rate performance 'Unsatisfactory'. What is the MAIN weakness?
opts: Lack of contemporaneous documentation to support the assessment
quiz.x: Evidence-based evaluations require contemporaneous records.

quiz.q: The government no longer needs a service due to a policy change, and the contractor has performed well. Which termination is appropriate?
quiz.x: Convenience termination applies when the government's needs change; it includes settlement for work performed.

quiz.q: Which document describes how the government will monitor a performance-based services contract?
quiz.x: The quality assurance surveillance plan sets surveillance methods and standards.

quiz.q: A proper invoice has been pending for 45 days without payment. What does the Prompt Payment Act generally require?
opts: Payment of interest penalties for late payment
quiz.x: Late payment of proper invoices generally triggers interest penalties.

modules.t: Day 3B — AI in Acquisition, Audit-Readiness & Capstone
modules.d: Using AI responsibly across the acquisition lifecycle, building audit-ready files, and your capstone.
modules.body:
AI in federal acquisition

The OECD, the World Bank and U.S. federal policymakers identify procurement as one of the most promising applications of AI in government — and one of the most sensitive for integrity. Federal policy issued in 2025 by the Office of Management and Budget (including memoranda on agencies' use and acquisition of AI) directs agencies to accelerate responsible AI adoption, manage risks for high-impact uses, and strengthen how they buy AI. Agencies are also building AI tools for acquisition workforce tasks. Use agency-approved tools only, and follow current OMB and agency guidance.

Where AI helps across the lifecycle

  • Requirements: drafting and reviewing PWS and SOO language for clarity, measurability and restrictive wording.
  • Market research: summarising capability statements, RFI responses and public information; identifying potential sources.
  • Solicitation: checking alignment between sections C, L and M; generating compliance matrices; drafting standard sections from templates.
  • Evaluation support: organising proposal content against criteria and checking evaluator narratives for consistency and documentation gaps.
  • Contract administration: summarising correspondence, tracking deliverables and deadlines, drafting letters and modification documents.
  • Knowledge work: explaining regulations, but always verified against current FAR and agency text.
Hard lines in acquisition. ① Source selection information and proprietary proposal data go only into tools specifically approved for that sensitivity — never public tools. ② AI must not make or determine award decisions, ratings or responsibility findings; humans with authority decide and document their reasoning. ③ AI-generated regulatory citations must be verified in the current FAR, RFO deviation text and agency supplements. ④ AI outputs used in the record are reviewed and owned by the responsible official.

Buying AI

When the government acquires AI systems, additional considerations apply: clear performance requirements and testing, data rights and ownership, protection of government data (including whether vendors may train on it), transparency and documentation, monitoring for drift and bias, security, avoiding vendor lock-in, and, for high-impact uses, risk management practices required by current federal policy. Performance-based requirements and staged, modular contracting help manage uncertainty.

Audit-readiness

Inspectors General, GAO and agency reviewers examine acquisition files. An audit-ready file (FAR 4.803 lists typical contents) tells the story of the acquisition: requirement and funding documents, acquisition plan, market research, J&As or set-aside decisions, IGCE, solicitation and amendments, proposals, evaluation records, competitive range and discussion records, price analysis, responsibility determination, award decision, debriefings, protests, modifications, surveillance records, performance evaluations, payments and closeout. Common findings include missing documents, unsupported price reasonableness determinations, inadequate trade-off documentation, unauthorized commitments, weak surveillance and late closeout.

Building an integrity culture

Strong acquisition organisations combine clear procedures with training, independent reviews, segregation of duties, ethics awareness, and leadership that supports contracting officers who say "no" to improper requests. Technology, including AI, should strengthen those controls, not bypass them.

Your capstone

Choose a realistic requirement from your environment. Produce: (1) a requirement summary and PWS or SOO extract with measurable standards; (2) a market research summary and set-aside decision; (3) a recommended method and contract type with justification; (4) aligned section L and M outlines; (5) a source selection plan with evaluation factors and trade-off approach; (6) a contract administration plan with QASP outline; (7) an AI-use statement describing approved tools, safeguards and human decision points; and (8) an audit-readiness checklist. Your instructor reviews it as a contracting officer and an auditor would.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my acquisition capstone reviewer, playing both an experienced contracting officer and an Inspector General auditor. I will paste my capstone package. Review each of the eight components for compliance with FAR principles, consistency between requirement, evaluation and administration, and documentation quality. Identify the top ten audit or protest risks, and remind me which current FAR, RFO deviation text, OMB guidance and agency rules I must verify.

📚 Glossary

  • Source selection information: protected information about the evaluation, not to be disclosed before award
  • Contract file: official record of the acquisition (FAR 4.803)
  • High-impact AI use: AI use with significant effects on rights or safety under federal policy
  • Modular contracting: acquiring systems in smaller, successive increments

📖 References

  • OMB memoranda on federal AI use and acquisition (2025) — whitehouse.gov/omb (verify current versions).
  • FAR 4.803 (contract file contents); FAR 3.104 (procurement integrity).
  • OECD — Recommendation on Public Procurement; OECD work on AI in public procurement.
  • GAO and agency Inspector General acquisition audit reports.

quiz.q: A contract specialist wants to paste offerors' technical proposals into a public AI chatbot to summarise them. What is the BEST response?
opts: Do not; proprietary proposal data and source selection information may only go into specifically approved tools
quiz.x: Protected proposal and source selection information must stay in approved systems.

quiz.q: An AI tool ranks proposals and recommends an awardee. What is the appropriate use?
opts: Use it at most as decision support; the source selection authority makes and documents an independent decision
Adopt the ranking as the award decision
Use it only for small contracts
Let the AI write the debriefing
quiz.x: Award decisions belong to officials with authority who document their reasoning.

quiz.q: An AI assistant cites 'FAR 15.306(d)(7)' for a discussion rule. What should the specialist do?
opts: Verify the citation in the current FAR, considering RFO deviation text and the agency supplement
quiz.x: Regulatory citations must be verified in current authoritative text.

quiz.q: Which is a common acquisition audit finding?
opts: Unsupported price reasonableness determinations or inadequate trade-off documentation
quiz.x: Missing price and trade-off support are frequent findings.

quiz.q: When the government buys an AI system that will process agency data, which contract issue is MOST important to address?
opts: Data rights and whether the vendor may use government data to train its models
quiz.x: Data rights and use protect government information and avoid unintended disclosure.

quiz.q: Which use of AI in acquisition is LOW risk and appropriate with approved tools?
opts: Determining responsibility of the apparent awardee
Checking alignment between sections C, L and M and generating a compliance matrix
quiz.x: Consistency checks support professionals without making authority decisions.

quiz.q: Why is modular or staged contracting useful when buying AI?
opts: It eliminates the need for requirements
It manages uncertainty by acquiring and testing capability in increments
quiz.x: Increments allow testing and adjustment, reducing risk.

quiz.q: An IG auditor asks why a J&A was not in the file for a sole-source award. What does this indicate?
opts: A significant documentation and possibly compliance failure for other than full and open competition
An administrative oversight with no consequence
quiz.x: Sole-source awards require documented justifications; their absence is a serious finding.

quiz.q: Which practice MOST strengthens integrity in an acquisition organisation?
opts: Allowing programme managers to direct contractors informally
Clear procedures, independent reviews, segregation of duties and leadership support for contracting officers
quiz.x: Integrity is built through controls, culture and leadership support.

quiz.q: Who owns AI-assisted content placed in the official contract file?
opts: The responsible official who reviewed and adopted it
quiz.x: Officials remain accountable for content in the official record.
